root_motivation: The target persona is an agent that ships tools in minutes (docs/agent-quickstart.md: signup→first publish 30.7 s median). Evidence: `on_tool_changed (republish/…)` in `python.rs:41` rebuilds the env and discards the old source; `grep -rniE 'tool_version|previous_version|version_history' src` finds nothing; `sharing.rs` lets tenant B call tenant A's tool by name with no version. Consequence: one wrong republish breaks a running workflow for its owner and for every sharer, with no undo short of pasting old source from a transcript.
user_persona: Any tenant or agent publishing idiomatic Python via host.tool_publish (e.g. PRD-fleet-bridge-live's fleet adapter, blocked live on 2026-09-12): the requirement inference must not reject `from __future__ import annotations` or `__main__` as unresolvable PyPI packages, since neither is installable and the publish error names something the calling agent cannot repair.

acceptance_criteria.description: Given a tool published twice, When `host.tool_history` is called, Then two versions are listed, version 2 current, with distinct `source_sha256`.
Given version 2 current, When `host.tool_rollback {version: 1}` is called, Then the next `host.tool_call` runs version 1's source.
Given a `free` tenant with 5 versions, When a sixth is published, Then version 1 is deleted and versions 2–6 remain.

scope: `infer-data/python-stdlib.json`: add `__future__` and `__main__` pseudo-module entries so requirement inference treats them as always-resolved, never-a-PyPI-package names (AC1/AC2).

`src/kinds/infer.rs`: the inference path that consumes the stdlib JSON, plus a `stdlib_regeneration_keeps_pseudo_modules` unit test asserting the pseudo-module entries survive a future list regeneration (AC4).

`tests/stdlibpseudo_ac1_future_import_empty_requirements.rs` and `tests/stdlibpseudo_ac2_dunder_main_no_requirement.rs`: sandboxed integration tests proving the real host.spec_test/host.tool_publish path end to end for AC1/AC2, wired into `tests/suite_sandbox_03.rs`.
non_goals: Re-generating the full stdlib list from a different source (separate concern, per the PRD's own Non-Goals).
Changing inference for genuinely unknown imports: those still error naming the import (AC3 regression guard, proven by the existing, unchanged AC10 coverage, reverified rather than duplicated).

additional.no_new_pypi_lookup: Pseudo-modules are recognized by name, not resolved against any package index -- the fix is an allowlist entry, not a network call.
additional.existing_ac10_unchanged: AC3's regression guard is proven by tests/ac10_publish_validation_errors.rs, already shipped and unmodified by this PRD; reverified, not re-implemented.

five_whys_trace.q: Why did PRD-fleet-bridge-live's AC6 live publish fail on 2026-09-12?
five_whys_trace.a: `host.tool_publish` rejected the fleet adapter's agent.py source with "cannot infer a PyPI requirement for import '__future__'".

five_whys_trace.q: Why did inference treat `__future__` as a PyPI requirement?
five_whys_trace.a: The requirement-inference path treats every import not listed in infer-data/python-stdlib.json as a third-party PyPI dependency, and that allowlist had no dunder/pseudo-module entries.

five_whys_trace.q: Why did the allowlist have no pseudo-module entries?
five_whys_trace.a: `__future__` and `__main__` are always-importable compiler/interpreter constructs, not real distributable packages -- nothing generates or installs them, so no stdlib-list source the allowlist was built from would ever list them.

five_whys_trace.q: Why is this more than one blocked publish?
five_whys_trace.a: `from __future__ import annotations` is present in most modern idiomatic Python, so any tenant publishing such source hits the identical, unrepairable publish error -- not a one-off.

five_whys_trace.q: Why does the fix add a regression test (AC4) rather than just the two allowlist entries?
five_whys_trace.a: The allowlist is a generated/maintained JSON file; a future regeneration from a different stdlib-list source has no reason to know these two names must survive, so a silent drop would reintroduce this exact failure with no test catching it.
